q: According to VSEPR theory, the shape of a BeCl₂ molecule is:
x: Be has two bond pairs and no lone pair, so the pairs lie on opposite sides of Be at 180°, giving a linear molecule.

q: A sigma (σ) bond is formed by:
o: Sideways overlap of two parallel p orbitals
Head-on (end-to-end) overlap of orbitals along the line joining the nuclei
Complete transfer of electrons from one atom to another
Overlap of two completely filled orbitals
x: A sigma bond forms by head-on overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis. Sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals gives a pi bond, and electron transfer gives an ionic bond.

q: Which of the following molecules is non-polar?
x: CO₂ is linear, so its two C=O bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel. H₂O (bent), NH₃ (pyramidal) and HCl all have a net dipole moment.

q: The ionic character of a covalent bond increases as:
o: The electronegativity difference between the bonded atoms increases
The electronegativity difference between the bonded atoms decreases
The two bonded atoms become identical
The number of shared electron pairs increases
x: The larger the electronegativity difference, the more the shared pair is pulled towards one atom, and the greater the partial charges and ionic character. Identical atoms give a pure covalent bond.

q: The F–B–F bond angle in a BF₃ molecule is:
x: Boron has three bond pairs and no lone pair. They spread out in one plane at 120°, giving a trigonal planar molecule.

q: How many sigma and pi bonds are present in one molecule of ethene, CH₂=CH₂?
x: There are four C–H sigma bonds, and the C=C double bond has one sigma and one pi bond. Total: 5 sigma and 1 pi.

q: Each C=O bond in CO₂ is polar, yet the CO₂ molecule has zero dipole moment. This is because:
o: Carbon and oxygen have the same electronegativity
The molecule is linear and the two bond dipoles cancel
The C=O bonds contain pi bonds
x: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so each bond is polar. But in the linear molecule the two equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions and their effects cancel.

q: Which bond has the greatest ionic character?
x: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so the electronegativity difference is greatest in H–F. Ionic character falls from H–F to H–I as halogen electronegativity decreases.

q: According to VSEPR theory, the strongest repulsion is between:
o: A lone pair and a bond pair
A bond pair and an inner-shell electron pair
x: The order of repulsion is lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair. Lone pairs are held by only one nucleus, so they spread out more and repel more strongly.

q: How many sigma and pi bonds are present in one molecule of ethyne, HC≡CH?
x: There are two C–H sigma bonds, and the C≡C triple bond has one sigma and two pi bonds. Total: 3 sigma and 2 pi.

q: Which of the following has a zero dipole moment?
x: In tetrahedral CCl₄ all four C–Cl bond dipoles are equal and symmetrically arranged, so they cancel. In the other three, unequal bonds (C–H and C–Cl) leave a net dipole.

q: An electronegativity difference of about 1.7 between two bonded atoms corresponds to roughly:
x: By the usual rule, a difference of about 1.7 gives a bond that is about 50% ionic. Above this the bond is mainly ionic; below it, mainly covalent.

q: The H–O–H bond angle in water (104.5°) is smaller than the H–C–H angle in methane (109.5°) because:
o: Oxygen is less electronegative than carbon
O–H bonds are much longer than C–H bonds
The two lone pairs on oxygen repel the bond pairs more strongly and push them closer
x: Both have four electron pairs around the central atom, but oxygen has two lone pairs. Lone pair repulsion is stronger than bond pair repulsion, so the O–H bond pairs are squeezed to 104.5°.

q: Which statement about a pi (π) bond is correct?
o: It can be formed by overlap of two s orbitals
It is formed before the sigma bond between two atoms
Its electron density lies above and below the line joining the nuclei
It allows free rotation of the bonded atoms
x: A pi bond comes from sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals, so its electron cloud lies above and below the internuclear axis. s orbitals cannot form pi bonds, a pi bond only forms after a sigma bond, and it prevents rotation.

q: BF₃ is non-polar but NH₃ is polar because:
o: B–F bonds are non-polar while N–H bonds are polar
BF₃ has a lone pair on boron
BF₃ is symmetrical and planar, while NH₃ is pyramidal with a lone pair
x: B–F bonds are polar, but in the symmetrical trigonal planar BF₃ the three dipoles cancel. NH₃ is pyramidal with a lone pair on N, so its bond dipoles do not cancel.

q: Which bond has no ionic character at all?
x: In Cl–Cl both atoms have the same electronegativity, so the electron pair is shared equally and the bond is purely covalent. Every bond between different atoms has some ionic character.

q: Which description of the PCl₅ molecule is correct?
o: Square pyramidal with all bond angles 90°
Trigonal bipyramidal with bond angles of 120° and 90°
Trigonal bipyramidal with all bond angles 120°
x: P has five bond pairs and no lone pair. Three Cl atoms lie in a plane at 120° and two lie above and below that plane at 90° to it, giving a trigonal bipyramid.

q: There is no free rotation about the C=C double bond in ethene because:
o: Rotation would destroy the sideways overlap of the p orbitals forming the pi bond
The sigma bond is broken by any rotation
The two carbon atoms are sp³ hybridised
The C=C bond contains two sigma bonds
x: The pi bond needs the two p orbitals to stay parallel. Twisting one carbon would break that sideways overlap, so rotation is restricted. A sigma bond alone is symmetrical about the axis and allows rotation.

q: Which of the following compounds has a zero dipole moment?
x: In trans-1,2-dichloroethene the two C–Cl bonds are on opposite sides of the double bond and point in opposite directions, so their dipoles cancel. In the cis and 1,1 forms both C–Cl dipoles point the same side.

q: In a molecule of hydrogen chloride, the partial charges are:
o: δ+ on chlorine and δ− on hydrogen
Full positive charge on hydrogen and full negative charge on chlorine
δ+ on hydrogen and δ− on chlorine
x: Chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen, so it pulls the shared pair closer and carries a partial negative charge (δ−); hydrogen carries δ+. The charges are partial because HCl is covalent, not ionic.

q: The shape of the SF₆ molecule is:
x: Sulphur has six bond pairs and no lone pair. Six pairs are farthest apart at the corners of an octahedron, with all F–S–F angles of 90°.

q: A sigma bond between two carbon atoms is stronger than a pi bond between them because:
o: A sigma bond contains more electrons than a pi bond
The extent of orbital overlap is greater in head-on overlap
A pi bond is formed from s orbitals
A sigma bond is formed by sideways overlap
x: Head-on overlap concentrates electron density directly between the nuclei and gives greater overlap than sideways overlap. Both bonds hold two electrons, so strength depends on the extent of overlap.

q: If the water molecule were linear like CO₂ instead of bent, its dipole moment would be:
o: Exactly the same as it is now
x: In a linear H–O–H the two equal O–H bond dipoles would point in opposite directions and cancel. Water is polar only because its bent shape stops this cancellation.

q: Which statement about a polar covalent bond is correct?
o: The shared pair is displaced towards the more electronegative atom
The electron pair is shared exactly equally
The electron pair is completely transferred to one atom
The shared pair is displaced towards the less electronegative atom
x: In a polar covalent bond the electrons are still shared, but unequally: the more electronegative atom pulls them closer and gains a partial negative charge. Complete transfer would make an ionic bond.

q: The correct order of bond angles is:
x: All three have four electron pairs. CH₄ has no lone pair (109.5°), NH₃ has one (107°) and H₂O has two (104.5°). More lone pairs squeeze the bond angle more.

q: Which compound contains ionic, normal covalent and coordinate covalent bonds in its solid?
x: NH₄Cl is made of NH₄⁺ and Cl⁻ ions (ionic bond); inside NH₄⁺ three N–H bonds are normal covalent and one formed when nitrogen's lone pair was donated to H⁺ (coordinate). CaCl₂ is only ionic, and NH₃ and CCl₄ only covalent; NH₃ tempts because it has a lone pair, but it has not yet donated it.

q: NH₃ and BF₃ combine to form the adduct H₃N–BF₃. The new N–B bond is formed when:
o: The lone pair on nitrogen is donated into the empty 2p orbital of boron
A lone pair on fluorine is donated into an empty orbital of nitrogen
Boron transfers one electron to nitrogen, forming ions
Nitrogen and boron each contribute one electron to the shared pair
x: Nitrogen in NH₃ has a lone pair, while boron in BF₃ has only six valence electrons and a vacant 2p orbital, so nitrogen donates the pair to boron: a coordinate (dative) bond. The tempting slip is to assume every covalent bond takes one electron from each atom.

q: Element P has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² and element Q has 1s² 2s² 2p⁵. The compound formed between them and its type of bonding are:
x: P (magnesium) loses its two 3s electrons to form P²⁺, and Q (fluorine) gains one electron to form Q⁻, so the formula is PQ₂. A metal of low ionisation energy with a very electronegative non-metal gives an ionic bond. P₂Q swaps the charges; PQ ignores the 2+ charge.

q: Solid metals conduct electricity because:
o: Their valence electrons are delocalised and free to move through the lattice of positive ions
Their positive ions move towards the negative terminal
Their atoms are joined by localised covalent bonds that carry the charge
They contain free protons that move through the crystal
x: In metallic bonding the valence electrons are not tied to any one atom; this mobile 'sea' of electrons carries the current while the cations stay fixed. Moving ions conduct only in molten or dissolved ionic compounds, which is the commonest mix-up.

q: The melting points of sodium, magnesium and aluminium increase in the order Na < Mg < Al. The main reason is that, from Na to Al:
o: The atoms become larger, so the forces between them increase
Each atom gives more electrons to the electron sea and the metal ions become smaller with a higher charge
The bonding changes from metallic to ionic
Fewer electrons are delocalised, so they are held more tightly
x: Na, Mg and Al give 1, 2 and 3 valence electrons per atom to the electron sea, and Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺ are smaller and more highly charged, so the attraction between the cations and the delocalised electrons (metallic bond strength) increases. The atoms actually get smaller across the period, so the 'larger atoms' reason is wrong.

q: In which molecule does the central atom have fewer than eight electrons in its valence shell?
x: Be has two valence electrons and forms two Be–Cl bonds, so only four electrons surround it. C in CCl₄ has four bond pairs, N in NCl₃ three bond pairs and one lone pair, and O in OCl₂ two bond pairs and two lone pairs: eight each. Forgetting lone pairs makes NCl₃ or OCl₂ look electron-deficient.

q: In the vapour at moderate temperatures, aluminium chloride exists as the dimer Al₂Cl₆. The two AlCl₃ units are held together by:
o: Ionic bonds between Al³⁺ and Cl⁻ ions
Two coordinate bonds, each from a lone pair on a chlorine atom to an aluminium atom
Two coordinate bonds, each from an aluminium atom to a chlorine atom
x: Aluminium in AlCl₃ has only six valence electrons and an empty orbital. A chlorine of one unit donates a lone pair to the aluminium of the other unit, and vice versa, giving two bridging coordinate bonds. Aluminium has no lone pair to give, so the reversed direction is wrong.

q: Solid X melts at 801 °C, does not conduct electricity as a solid but conducts when molten, and dissolves in water. Liquid Y freezes at −23 °C and does not conduct in any state. The bonding in X and Y is best described as:
o: X ionic; Y covalent, made of separate molecules
X covalent, made of separate molecules; Y metallic
x: Conduction only when molten means ions that are fixed in the solid and free in the melt, so X is ionic (it behaves like NaCl). A low melting point and no conduction in any state point to small separate molecules held by weak forces, so Y is molecular covalent (like CCl₄). A covalent network solid would not conduct even when molten.

q: The ammonium ion NH₄⁺ has four N–H bonds. How many electrons in total are shared in these bonds, and how many of them came from the nitrogen atom?
x: Four bonds hold 4 × 2 = 8 electrons. Three H atoms give one electron each and H⁺ gives none, so nitrogen supplies 8 − 3 = 5: one to each of three normal bonds plus both electrons of the coordinate bond. Counting only the normal bonds gives 3; forgetting that H⁺ has no electron gives 4.

q: Which of these period 2 elements has the highest first ionisation energy?
x: First ionisation energy generally rises across period 2, but oxygen is below nitrogen: N (2p³) has a stable half-filled 2p subshell, while in O (2p⁴) one 2p orbital holds a pair whose repulsion makes an electron easier to remove. So N > O > C > B; choosing O follows the general trend and misses this exception.

q: The first electron affinity of chlorine (−349 kJ mol⁻¹) is more exothermic than that of fluorine (−328 kJ mol⁻¹), although fluorine is more electronegative. The main reason is that:
o: Chlorine has a complete octet before it gains an electron
Fluorine already has a full 2p subshell
The electron added to chlorine enters a 3d orbital
Fluorine is very small, so the incoming electron is strongly repelled by the electrons crowded in its 2p subshell
x: The added electron goes into 2p for F and 3p for Cl. The compact 2p subshell of fluorine is crowded, so electron–electron repulsion cancels part of the nuclear attraction and less energy is released. Neither atom has a full subshell before gaining the electron (both are ns² np⁵), and the electron for Cl enters 3p, not 3d.

q: Using Pauling electronegativities H 2.1, C 2.5, N 3.0, O 3.5 and Cl 3.0, which bond is the least polar?
x: Polarity follows the electronegativity difference: N–Cl 0, C–Cl 0.5, O–Cl 0.5, H–Cl 0.9. N–Cl has no difference, so it is the least polar. Choosing H–Cl or C–Cl comes from assuming any bond to Cl is polar without comparing the values.

q: In which pair do both species have the same shape according to VSEPR theory?
x: NH₃ and H₃O⁺ each have three bond pairs and one lone pair on the central atom, so both are trigonal pyramidal. BF₃ (three bond pairs, no lone pair) is trigonal planar but PH₃ is pyramidal; SO₂ has a lone pair on S and is bent while CO₂ is linear; NH₄⁺ is tetrahedral. Ignoring lone pairs makes BF₃ and PH₃ look alike.

q: In which molecule is the central atom sp³ hybridised, yet the molecule is not tetrahedral in shape?
x: Oxygen in H₂O has two bond pairs and two lone pairs, so it uses four sp³ hybrid orbitals, but only the two O–H bonds define the shape, which is bent. CH₄ is sp³ and tetrahedral; BF₃ is sp² (trigonal planar) and BeCl₂ is sp (linear). Confusing hybridisation with shape leads to CH₄.

q: In pent-3-en-1-yne, CH₃–CH=CH–C≡CH, how many carbon atoms are sp hybridised and how many are sp² hybridised?
x: The CH₃ carbon is sp³; the two carbons of C=C are sp²; both carbons of C≡C are sp. That gives 2 sp and 2 sp². Counting only the terminal ≡CH as sp, or only one carbon of each multiple bond, gives the wrong counts.

q: According to molecular orbital theory, which of these molecules is paramagnetic?
x: O₂ has two unpaired electrons in its two π*2p orbitals, so it is attracted into a magnetic field. N₂, F₂ and H₂ have all electrons paired. A simple Lewis structure of O₂ shows all electrons paired, which is why its paramagnetism needs MOT.

q: According to molecular orbital theory, a stable He₂ molecule does not exist because:
o: Its filled 1s orbitals cannot overlap at all
Its bond order would be 2, too strong to be stable
It would have two electrons in the bonding orbital and two in the antibonding orbital, giving a bond order of zero
Helium atoms are too large to approach each other
x: Four electrons fill σ1s² σ*1s², so bond order = (2 − 2)/2 = 0 and there is no net bonding. Filled orbitals can overlap; the point is that the antibonding electrons cancel the bonding ones. Helium atoms are in fact very small.

q: According to molecular orbital theory, what are the bond order of N₂ and, counting all 14 electrons (1s included), the number of electrons in antibonding orbitals?
x: N₂ has 14 electrons: bonding σ1s², σ2s², π2p⁴, σ2p² (10) and antibonding σ*1s², σ*2s² (4). Bond order = (10 − 4)/2 = 3. Forgetting the σ*1s pair gives 2 antibonding electrons; assuming a triple bond means no antibonding electrons gives 0.

q: In the O₂ molecule, the two unpaired electrons occupy:
o: The two degenerate π*2p antibonding orbitals, one electron in each
The two π2p bonding orbitals, one electron in each
x: After σ2s², σ*2s², σ2p², π2p⁴ are filled, O₂ has two more valence electrons; by Hund's rule they go singly into the two equal-energy π*2p orbitals. The π2p bonding orbitals are already full, and σ*2p is higher in energy and empty.

q: The hydrogen molecule ion H₂⁺ has only one electron. According to molecular orbital theory, its bond order and stability are:
o: 1; it is as stable as H₂
0.5; it can exist, but its bond is weaker than in H₂
0.5; it cannot exist because the bond order is not a whole number
x: The single electron is in σ1s, so bond order = (1 − 0)/2 = 0.5. Any positive bond order means a bond, so H₂⁺ exists, but half the bond order of H₂ gives a weaker bond. A fractional bond order does not stop a species existing.

q: According to molecular orbital theory, the F₂ molecule has:
x: F₂ has 14 valence electrons: σ2s², σ*2s², σ2p², π2p⁴, π*2p⁴. Bond order = (8 − 6)/2 = 1, and the π* orbitals are completely filled, so all electrons are paired (diamagnetic). Carrying over the paramagnetism of O₂ gives the wrong magnetic behaviour.

q: Arrange O₂, the superoxide ion O₂⁻ and the peroxide ion O₂²⁻ in order of increasing O–O bond energy.
x: Each extra electron enters a π*2p antibonding orbital: bond orders are O₂ 2, O₂⁻ 1.5, O₂²⁻ 1. A higher bond order means a stronger bond, so O₂²⁻ < O₂⁻ < O₂. Thinking that extra electrons strengthen the bond reverses the order.

q: One electron is removed from N₂ to form N₂⁺, and one from O₂ to form O₂⁺. How do the bond lengths of the ions compare with those of the neutral molecules?
o: Both ions have shorter bonds than their molecules
Both ions have longer bonds than their molecules
N₂⁺ is longer than N₂, but O₂⁺ is shorter than O₂
N₂⁺ is shorter than N₂, but O₂⁺ is longer than O₂
x: N₂ loses a bonding electron (bond order 3 → 2.5), so its bond lengthens; O₂ loses an antibonding π*2p electron (bond order 2 → 2.5), so its bond shortens. Assuming that removing any electron has the same effect gives one of the 'both' options.

q: Which order of bond energy for the hydrogen halides is correct?
x: From F to I the halogen atom gets larger, so the H–X bond gets longer and the overlap weaker; bond energy falls (about 568, 432, 366 and 298 kJ mol⁻¹). The reverse order comes from thinking larger atoms form stronger bonds.

q: The measured dipole moment of a diatomic molecule XY is 1.2 D. If the X–Y bond were completely ionic, its dipole moment would be 6.0 D. What is the percentage ionic character of the bond?
x: Percentage ionic character = (observed ÷ fully ionic value) × 100 = (1.2 ÷ 6.0) × 100 = 20%. Taking 100 − 20 gives 80%, which is the covalent share; dividing the wrong way round (6.0 ÷ 1.2 = 5) gives 5%.
